The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. ## Abstract
Legal disputes over laws that require certain forms of identification (ID) to vote mostly focus on the burden placed on people who do not possess ID.
We contend that this singular focus ignores the burden imposed on people who do possess ID, but nonetheless cannot access it when voting.
To measure this alternative conception of burden, we focus on Michigan, which allows anyone who lacks access to ID to vote after signing an affidavit.
A sample of affidavits filed in the 2016 presidential election from a random set of precincts reveals that about 0.45 percent of voters lacked access to ID.
Consistent with our broader conception of the burden of voter ID laws, nearly all voters who filed an affidavit were previously issued a still‐active state ID.
Importantly, we show minority voters were about five times more likely to lack access to ID than white voters.
We also present survey evidence suggesting that people who live in states where voters are asked to show ID, as in Michigan, are more likely to incorrectly believe that access to ID is required to vote than are people who live in states that do not ask voters to show ID.

Are these partisan views on the impact of voter ID correct?
Existing research focuses on how voter ID laws affect voter turnout and fraud.
But the extent to which they produce observable electoral benefits for Republican candidates and/or penalize Democrats remains an open question.
We examine how voter ID impacts the parties’ electoral fortunes in races at the state level (state legislatures and governorships) and federal level (United States Congress and president) during 2003 to 2020.
Our results suggest negligible average effects but with some heterogeneity over time.
The first laws implemented produced a Democratic advantage, which weakened to near zero after 2012.
We conclude that voter ID requirements motivate and mobilize supporters of both parties, ultimately mitigating their anticipated effects on election results.

In recent years, voter ID laws and convenience voting have generated heated partisan debates.
To shed light on these policy issues, we survey the evidence on the institutional determinants and effects of voter turnout and broaden the perspective beyond the most debated rules.
We begin by discussing the importance of electoral participation both for its consequences on policy choices and for democratic legitimacy.
Building on a simple cost–benefit model of voting, we then review (quasi-)experimental research on the effects of voting procedures and of other election rules.
Voting procedures primarily affect the cost of participation.
The obstacles they create matter more when they occur ahead of the election and when the stakes are not salient, and they matter less when parties mobilize voters against them and when alternative ways to vote exist.

Whereas in past elections approximately 1-2% of mail ballots in Texas were rejected,17 counties reported rejection rates of between 6-22% in the 2022 Texas Primary: County Vote by mail rejection rate in 2022 Texas Primary Bexar18 22% (approximately 4,000 ballots) Collin19 13.7% (828 ballots) Dallas20 6.5% (694 ballots) El Paso21 16% (725 ballots) Harris22 19% (6,919 ballots) Hays23 8.2% (208 ballots) Hidalgo24 19.4% (526 ballots) Travis25 8% (approximately 900 ballots) Williamson26 11.5% (521 ballots) ... And we know that this explosion in the number of rejected mail ballots is a d 9. Restrictive Mail Voting Rules Burden Minority Voters ... https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/2024-03/Miller%20-%20Texas_Rejections.pdf One particularly onerous aspect of SB1 was a requirement that voters know whether they originally registered to vote with their driver’s license or social security number to vote by mail; if they used the wrong number, their mail application or ballot would be rejected. We show that this led to ballot rejection rates in excess of 10% in the 2022 primary, with large racial discrepancies—white voters had their applications and ballots rejected at far lower rates. ... Beginning in 2022 elections, voters were required to submit either their state identification number or a partial social security number on their application for mailed ballots, and then again on the underside of the ballot envelope flap upon submitting it. ... The preliminary results from this paper make clear that SB1 substantially increased the rate at which applications to vote by mail, and mail ballots themselves, were rejected in the 2022 primary elections in Texas. More than 30,000 Texans who began the process of trying to cast a ballot were prevented from doing so. More than 10% of all mail ballots cast in the primary were rejected due to this provision, a rejection rate that is virtually unheard of. As we show, there were extremely large racial disparities in the rejection rates of these ballots and applications; Asian, Black, and Latino voters were all almost 50% more likely to have their ballots rejected than white voters. 10. Nearly 25,000 mail ballots were rejected in Texas primary https://www.newsweek.com/mail-ballots-rejected-texas-primary-election-voting-1695868 Texas threw out almost 25,000 mail-in ballots in the March primary, according to figures released by the Texas secretary of state.A total of 24,636 mail ballots were rejected in the state's 254 counties in the first election held since sweeping changes to Texas' voting rules were signed into law by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in 2021.The rejection rate was about 12.4 percent, far higher than previous elections. ... Sergio Flores/Getty Images The rejection rate was similar for those trying to cast ballots in the Democrat and Republican primaries—about 12.9 percent (14,281) of Democratic ballots were rejected compared to 11.8 percent (10,355) of Republican ballots, according to The Texas Tribune." The only reason that the rejection rate soared this high is that Senate Bill 1 imposed this new ID requirement and it is disenfranchising eligible voters," said James Slattery, a senior staff attorney at the Texas Civil Rights Project.Republicans had raced to put the law tightening voting rules on the books in time for the 2022 midterm elections, partly driven by former President Donald Trump's persistent and baseless claims of rampant fraud in the 2020 election.The new law requires voters to list an identification number—from their driver's license or the last four digits of their Social Security number—on their mail ballot application and return envelope.That number must match the number on file with their voter registration records.

STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB
Protect your voice
Protect our vote
Trump’s allies want to take away our vote to silence our voice and rig California elections so they can keep control of Congress and the White House. They want to make voting in California harder, less secure, and more expensive. Trump will do whatever it takes to take away our right to vote, dodge accountability, and hold onto authoritarian power.
Californians won’t fall for it. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop 39.
Learn
more
about
Prop 39
WASTES HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS.
Trump and his accomplices want California to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to chase their election lies and conspiracy theories. Californians are struggling, and Trump wants YOU to pay for indulging his election denial conspiracies.
PUTS YOUR IDENTITY AT RISK.
Prop 39 will make every vote by mail voter write their personal details on their return envelope – making voters easy targets for identity theft. Voters would have to choose between voting and protecting their privacy.
BLOCKS CITIZENS FROM VOTING.
Prop 39 adds new hurdles – voters would have to write a personal ID number on their ballot envelope that has to exactly match state records. Get one digit wrong, and a valid ballot may get thrown out. If you don’t take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting – you may not get a mail ballot at all. And if the address on your ID is not up to date or your name is misspelled – your vote might be rejected.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. ## Abstract
Legal disputes over laws that require certain forms of identification (ID) to vote mostly focus on the burden placed on people who do not possess ID.
We contend that this singular focus ignores the burden imposed on people who do possess ID, but nonetheless cannot access it when voting.
To measure this alternative conception of burden, we focus on Michigan, which allows anyone who lacks access to ID to vote after signing an affidavit.
A sample of affidavits filed in the 2016 presidential election from a random set of precincts reveals that about 0.45 percent of voters lacked access to ID.
Consistent with our broader conception of the burden of voter ID laws, nearly all voters who filed an affidavit were previously issued a still‐active state ID.
Importantly, we show minority voters were about five times more likely to lack access to ID than white voters.
We also present survey evidence suggesting that people who live in states where voters are asked to show ID, as in Michigan, are more likely to incorrectly believe that access to ID is required to vote than are people who live in states that do not ask voters to show ID.

last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

All states have voter identification requirements, ranging from simply providing one's name to showing an official photo ID.
Rules vary widely state by state, and voter ID has been a source of political and legal controversy in the United States for nearly two decades.
Supporters of more stringent voter ID requirements argue they will deter voter fraud and instill confidence in the integrity of the electoral process.
Opponents argue that voter fraud is extremely rare, so the only effect of such requirements is to raise the barriers to voting in ways that disproportionately affect citizens of low socioeconomic status.
The implementation of strict voter ID requirements in recent years has led to several lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and an increase in scholarly research into the effects of these laws on voter turnout.

## Research on voter ID
One topic of particular interest has been the disparate impact photo ID laws may have on racial minority groups and turnout.
Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute.
Some scholars have found a decrease in racial minority turnout nationwide, but other studies have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an *increase* in youth turnout.
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear.

All states have voter identification requirements, ranging from simply providing one's name to showing an official photo ID.
Rules vary widely state by state, and voter ID has been a source of political and legal controversy in the United States for nearly two decades.
Supporters of more stringent voter ID requirements argue they will deter voter fraud and instill confidence in the integrity of the electoral process.
Opponents argue that voter fraud is extremely rare, so the only effect of such requirements is to raise the barriers to voting in ways that disproportionately affect citizens of low socioeconomic status.
The implementation of strict voter ID requirements in recent years has led to several lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and an increase in scholarly research into the effects of these laws on voter turnout.

## Research on voter ID
One topic of particular interest has been the disparate impact photo ID laws may have on racial minority groups and turnout.
Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute.
Some scholars have found a decrease in racial minority turnout nationwide, but other studies have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an *increase* in youth turnout.
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear.

last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. All states have voter identification requirements, ranging from simply providing one's name to showing an official photo ID.
Rules vary widely state by state, and voter ID has been a source of political and legal controversy in the United States for nearly two decades.
Supporters of more stringent voter ID requirements argue they will deter voter fraud and instill confidence in the integrity of the electoral process.
Opponents argue that voter fraud is extremely rare, so the only effect of such requirements is to raise the barriers to voting in ways that disproportionately affect citizens of low socioeconomic status.
The implementation of strict voter ID requirements in recent years has led to several lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and an increase in scholarly research into the effects of these laws on voter turnout.

Our recent paper discusses a randomized field experiment we designed to assess the effects of providing informational reminders about voter ID requirements to registered voters in Virginia’s general election in November, 2017.
We examine the effects of our interventions on voter turnout in the election unobtrusively, using validated voting records obtained following the election, but we also consider whether our treatments influenced attitudes about voter ID laws, perceptions of electoral fraud, and other aspects of elections by contacting subjects after the election to solicit their views on these topics in a short-automated telephone survey.

First, we obtained official voter turnout records for the November 2017 elections following the election.
We also conducted a post-election survey, which was relatively brief; it contained between 13 and 15 questions depending on responses provided.
The survey probed respondents about perceptions of fraud, satisfaction with democracy, and self-assessed and actual knowledge of Virginia voting requirements.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Summary
Support
Supporters argue that ID requirements at voting sites will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, and that most states require voters to show some form of identification to vote.
Oppose
Opponents say requiring ID will make it harder for eligible voters who don’t have a driver’s license or other supporting documents to vote. They say this will disproportionately affect those with disabilities, who are low-income or have recently moved.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

All states have voter identification requirements, ranging from simply providing one's name to showing an official photo ID. Rules vary widely state by state, and voter ID has been a source of political and legal controversy in the United States for nearly two decades.
Supporters of more stringent voter ID requirements argue they will deter voter fraud and instill confidence in the integrity of the electoral process. Opponents argue that voter fraud is extremely rare, so the only effect of such requirements is to raise the barriers to voting in ways that disproportionately affect citizens of low socioeconomic status.
The implementation of strict voter ID requirements in recent years has led to several lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and an increase in scholarly research into the effects of these laws on voter turnout.
This explainer was last updated on June 24, 2026.
Current requirements
Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act (HAVA), first-time voters in federal elections in every state must show some form of ID at the polls if they registered by mail (they do not need to show ID if they registered in person). States are allowed to augment identification requirements beyond this “HAVA minimum” for all voters, first-time or not.
States with HAVA-minimum requirements typically require voters to announce their name and address at a check-in table when they vote in person. Many of these states also require the voter to sign in. Falsely claiming to be a registered voter is voter impersonation fraud and is a felony in most states.
The National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) has created a useful two-dimensional classification system (http://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id.aspx) to describe the types of voter identification requirements for states that go beyond the HAVA minimum. The first dimension is whether the state requires the voter to show an ID with a photograph. The second dimension is whether a voter without proper ID is required to cast a provisional ballot and then take some additional steps after Election Day to have the ballot counted (“strict” states), or whether such a voter can sign an affidavit attesting to his or her identity and cast a regular ballot on Election Day (“non-strict” states).
