PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39
VOTE NO. Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.
STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. CALIFORNIANS WON’T FALL FOR IT. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop. 39. Don’t let California become the next state where politicians pick which voters count.

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Findings and Purposes.
To enforce existing voter qualifications, including US
citizenship, established by California’s Constitution,
the people hereby amend the California Constitution:
(A) to promote public confidence and trust in the
electoral process, which encourages civic participation
and supports a healthy democracy; (B) to deter and
detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter
registration records and confirming eligibility to vote;
and (C) to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by
requiring proof of identity to vote.

SEC. 2.1. Section 3.1 is added to Article II of the
California Constitution, to read:
SEC. 3.1. (a) The Secretary of State, and county
elections officials, shall each have the duty to maintain
accurate voter registration lists, shall use best efforts to
verify citizenship attestations using government data,
and shall annually report what percentage of each
county’s voter rolls have been citizenship-verified.
(b) Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any
election in the State, the voter shall present
government-issued identification, or if voting by mail,
the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique
identifying number from government-issued
identification that matches the one designated by the
voter for their voter registration. The type of
identification designated by each voter must be
indicated in their voter registration record, noted on the
mail ballot envelope provided to them, and available to
them on request by phone or electronically. Election
officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot
after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant
to the requirements of this section, and verifying that
the person has cast only one ballot in the election.
Government-issued identification means
documentation that allows conclusive verification of the
voter’s identity. Upon request by an eligible voter, the
State shall provide, at no charge, a voter ID card for use
in casting a ballot.
(c) This section shall be self-executing. The Legislature
shall also promptly enact laws to implement this
section, provide for voting by military and overseas
voters consistent with federal law, and ensure that all
State and local officials comply and support the
compliance with this section. Citizens may seek judicial
review and remedy of the State’s or any county’s
compliance with this section. During every odd-
numbered year, the California State Auditor shall audit
the State’s and each county’s compliance with this
section and report its findings and recommendations
for improving the integrity of elections to the public.
SEC. 3. Severability.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any portion,
section, subdivision, paragraph, clause, sentence,
phrase, word, or application of this act is for any reason
held to be invalid by a decision of any court of
competent jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect
the validity of the remaining portions of this act, which
shall be given effect without the invalid portion or
application.
PROPOSITION 40
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds a section to the California
Constitution and amends and adds sections to the
Government Code and Revenue and Taxation Code;
therefore, new provisions proposed to be added are
printed in italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED LAW
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.
(d) The loss of billions in federal funding further
stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to
reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source
of health coverage for half of all births statewide.
Recent years have seen closures of vital maternity
wards and emergency departments, all attributed in
large part to low Medi-Cal reimbursement rates.
(g) Investment in Medi-Cal is an investment in every
family’s health security. It keeps primary care clinics
and community health centers open across towns and
cities, allowing people to manage chronic conditions,
prevent costly complications, and live longer, healthier
lives. Every dollar cut from these programs

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. # Who Votes Without Identification? Using Individual‐Level Administrative Data to Measure the Burden of Strict Voter Identification Laws
...
## Abstract
Legal disputes over laws that require certain forms of identification (ID) to vote mostly focus on the burden placed on people who do not possess ID.
We contend that this singular focus ignores the burden imposed on people who do possess ID, but nonetheless cannot access it when voting.
To measure this alternative conception of burden, we focus on Michigan, which allows anyone who lacks access to ID to vote after signing an affidavit.
A sample of affidavits filed in the 2016 presidential election from a random set of precincts reveals that about 0.45 percent of voters lacked access to ID.
Consistent with our broader conception of the burden of voter ID laws, nearly all voters who filed an affidavit were previously issued a still‐active state ID.
Importantly, we show minority voters were about five times more likely to lack access to ID than white voters.
We also present survey evidence suggesting that people who live in states where voters are asked to show ID, as in Michigan, are more likely to incorrectly believe that access to ID is required to vote than are people who live in states that do not ask voters to show ID.

Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

All states have voter identification requirements, ranging from simply providing one's name to showing an official photo ID. Rules vary widely state by state, and voter ID has been a source of political and legal controversy in the United States for nearly two decades.
Supporters of more stringent voter ID requirements argue they will deter voter fraud and instill confidence in the integrity of the electoral process. Opponents argue that voter fraud is extremely rare, so the only effect of such requirements is to raise the barriers to voting in ways that disproportionately affect citizens of low socioeconomic status.
The implementation of strict voter ID requirements in recent years has led to several lawsuits alleging racial discrimination and an increase in scholarly research into the effects of these laws on voter turnout.
This explainer was last updated on June 24, 2026.
Current requirements
Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act (HAVA), first-time voters in federal elections in every state must show some form of ID at the polls if they registered by mail (they do not need to show ID if they registered in person). States are allowed to augment identification requirements beyond this “HAVA minimum” for all voters, first-time or not.
States with HAVA-minimum requirements typically require voters to announce their name and address at a check-in table when they vote in person. Many of these states also require the voter to sign in. Falsely claiming to be a registered voter is voter impersonation fraud and is a felony in most states.
The National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) has created a useful two-dimensional classification system (http://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id.aspx) to describe the types of voter identification requirements for states that go beyond the HAVA minimum. The first dimension is whether the state requires the voter to show an ID with a photograph. The second dimension is whether a voter without proper ID is required to cast a provisional ballot and then take some additional steps after Election Day to have the ballot counted (“strict” states), or whether such a voter can sign an affidavit attesting to his or her identity and cast a regular ballot on Election Day (“non-strict” states).
Close
The following map summarizes voter ID laws as of July 2025. As a general matter, the strictest ID laws are in the South and Great Lakes states; the least strict laws are in the Northeast and the West Coast.
Close
Note that this explainer provides an overall summary of voter ID policy. Individual state voter ID laws are quite detailed and vary widely, so if you are interested in the details of voter ID laws in your state, consult your state’s resources or local election officials.
In general, voter ID laws only apply to those who vote in person (with the exception of first-time voters who register by mail, who under HAVA requirements must include a photocopy of their identification if they vote for the first time by mail). The identification of voters who cast their ballots by mail, whether they use a traditional absentee or vote-by-mail ballot, is typically handled by matching the signature on the outer return envelope with the voter signature election officials have on file.
Legal controversy
Before the 2000 election, there was far less public focus on voter ID laws. Most states had what are now known as HAVA-minimum requirements, although some had non-strict, non-photo ID laws.
Following the controversies surrounding the 2000 presidential election, photo ID requirements were given a boost by two efforts. First, Democratic sponsors of HAVA agreed to stipulations made by their Republican counterparts around ID provisions pertaining to first-time voters in order to secure the legislation’s passage in the Senate. Second, in its 2005 report (https://www.eac.gov/assets/1/6/Exhibit%20M.PDF), the Commission on Federal Election Reform (known as the Carter-Baker Commission) recommended that all states institute photo ID requirements.
In 2005, Indiana was the first state to pass a strict voter photo ID requirement. The law was immediately challenged by the Marion County (Indianapolis) Democratic Central Committee as imposing an undue burden on voting rights under the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Both the federal trial court and the circuit court of appeals rejected these claims. The U.S. Supreme Court subsequently agreed to hear the case, and in Crawford v. Marion County Election Board (http://www.scotusblog.com/case-files/cases/crawford-v-marion-county-election-bd/), ruled that states had a reasonable interest in preventing election fraud and that photo ID laws were not, on their face, unconstitutional.
The 2008 Crawford decision was seen as a green light both to supporters and opponents of stricter ID laws. To supporters, Crawford signaled that “reasonable (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/553/181/)” ID requirements, motivated by a desire to prevent voter fraud, would likely be found constitutional. To opponents (https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/aclu-disappointed-supreme-courts-voter-id-decision), the Crawford decision laid out a possible path for future challenges. While the Supreme Court ruled that photo ID laws were not unconstitutional on their face, it did signal that if opponents could show specific harms to voters that outweighed states’ interests in curbing fraud, strict voter ID laws might be struck down.
The number of states with some form of voter ID requirement rose significantly between the presidential elections of 2004 and 2008 (see Figure 2). The fastest-growing categories of ID laws involve photo identification, although most states with photo ID requirements still fall into the “non-strict” category.
Close
In 2013, another Supreme Court case spurred passage of strict photo ID laws: Shelby County v. Holder , a case related to the federal pre-clearance provisions of the Voting Rights Act (VRA). Prior to Shelby County, states “covered” under Section 5 of the VRA (primarily states with a history of racially discriminatory barriers to participation) were required to have any election-related voting procedure changes pre-cleared by the Justice Department. To be granted pre-clearance, a state covered by Section 5 would have to show that an ID law did not make minority voters worse off in their “effective exercise of the electoral franchise (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-28/part-51#p-51.54(b)).” Although Section 5 was not a hard stop on the passage of stricter photo ID requirements — Georgia’s strict photo ID law, for example, was precleared by the Department of Justice in 2006 — it made the process more complicated for states that might have otherwise attempted to pass them. In Shelby County , the Court ultimately decided that the coverage formula outlined in Section 4 of the VRA was outdated, effectively gutting the pre-clearance provision. This decision made it easier for states that had previously been subject to pre-clearance to adopt stricter ID laws. Several states, including North Carolina and Texas, moved quickly to enact photo ID laws that were much stricter than those from the previous decade.
Since Shelby County , the Supreme Court has not agreed to hear additional cases relating to voter ID, instead letting rulings from lower courts stand. In 2017, the Supreme Court declined to hear a case from the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals. This allowed the lower court’s decision to strike down the voter ID requirement enacted by North Carolina in 2013 to stand. The Supreme Court also allowed the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision to loosen Texas’ 2011 strict voter ID law to stand by declining to hear the case Veasey v. Abbott .
State supreme courts have weighed in more actively on voter ID. The North Carolina Supreme Court upheld a stricter voter ID law ( Holmes v. Moore) in 2023, while the Montana Supreme Court upheld a decision in 2024 that struck down a state law limiting acceptable voter ID ( Montana Democratic Party v. Jacobsen) .
More legislative changes to voter ID law and election administration resulted from the 2020 presidential election, in which many Americans opted to vote by mail due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The election spurred an expansion of vote by mail eligibility throughout the country; subsequently, this expansion also fed concerns about potential increases in voter fraud because of the increase in absentee ballots. As a consequence of the increased skepticism about the security of absentee ballots, several Republican-controlled legislatures have since enacted or increased identification requirements for mail ballots. These new laws did not always focus on photo ID. In 2021, for example, Georgia (SB 202 (https://www.legis.ga.gov/legislation/59827)), Florida (SB 90 (https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2021/90)), and Montana (SB 169 (https://legiscan.com/MT/bill/SB169/2025)) all passed bills requiring that voters returning mail ballots supply their driver’s license number or the last four digits of their Social Security number.
In another trend, states have begun to pass legislation changing the types of acceptable identification voters can provide. Between 2021 and 2025, Missouri (HB 1878 (https://house.mo.gov/Bill.aspx?bill=HB1878&year=2022&code=R)), Nebraska (Initiative 432 (https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2022/Pamphlet%20for%20Initiatives%20432%20%26%20433.pdf)), Ohio (HB 458 (https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/134/hb458)), New Hampshire (HB 1569 (https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/legacy/bs2016/bill_status.aspx?lsr=2111&sy=2024&sortoption=&txtsessionyear=2024&txtbillnumber=HB1569)), and West Virginia (HB 3016 (https://www.wvlegislature.gov/bill_status/bills_history.cfm?INPUT=3016&year=2025&sessiontype=RS)) all enacted legislation requiring photo IDs. All of these states previously required a non-photo ID except for Nebraska, which did not previously have any identification requirements except for the HAVA minimum. Some states have also passed legislation that determines whether student IDs are an acceptable method of identification. Idaho (HB 124 (https://legislature.idaho.gov/sessioninfo/2023/legislation/H0124/)) and Indiana (SB 10 (https://iga.in.gov/legislative/2025/bills/senate/10/details)), for example, have removed it from their list of valid IDs, while Montana (SB 267 (https://legiscan.com/MT/bill/SB267/2025)) has added certain photo student IDs.
Other states have turned to direct democracy, putting voter ID measures on the ballot (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_ID_policy_ballot_measures#important2024datesbanner-spanstylefontsize105yearsspan-1). Since 2018, voters in Arkansas (Arkansas Issue 2, Voter ID Amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/Arkansas_Issue_2,_Voter_ID_Amendment_(2018))), North Carolina (North Carolina Voter ID Amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Voter_ID_Amendment_(2018))), Nebraska (Nebraska Initiative 432, Photo Voter Identification Initiative (https://ballotpedia.org/Nebraska_Initiative_432,_Photo_Voter_Identification_Initiative_(2022))), Michigan (Ballot Proposal 2 of 2022 (https://www.house.mi.gov/hfa/PDF/Alpha/Ballot_Proposal_2_of_2022.pdf)), Nevada (Nevada Question 7, Require Voter Identification Initiative (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_7,_Require_Voter_Identification_Initiative_(2024))), and Wisconsin (Wisconsin Question 1, Require Voter Photo ID Amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/Wisconsin_Question_1,_Require_Voter_Photo_ID_Amendment_(April_2025))) have passed ballot measures creating stricter voter ID requirements, such as requiring voters to present a photo ID. Arizona (2022) and Maine (2025) have also had referenda on the ballot requiring stricter voter ID, but these measures did not pass.
At the federal level, the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act (https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/22) (H.R. 22) was introduced in January 2025 and passed the House of Representatives on April 10, 2025 by a vote of 220–208, largely along party lines, after which it was received in the Senate but did not advance. The act called for Americans to provide documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and mandated the removal of noncitizens from voter rolls. In early 2026, House Republicans proposed a new version, the SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296). (https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7296)On February 11, 2026, the House approved an amendment to S. 1383 by a vote of 218–213 that substituted in text mirroring the SAVE America Act. The Senate began procedural consideration in March 2026, though its path to the 60 votes needed remains uncertain as of writing. Both build on an earlier predecessor, H.R. 8281 (https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/8281), which passed the House in 2024 but died in the Senate despite attempts to attach it to a government funding measure. While the original bill focused primarily on documentary proof of citizenship at registration, the 2026 SAVE America Act added a requirement to present a specified voter ID to cast a ballot, along with voter roll maintenance provisions.
Research on voter ID
Voter ID has also been the subject of intense scrutiny by scholars. One topic of particular interest has been the disparate impact photo ID laws may have on racial minority groups and turnout. Research on this issue is the topic of ongoing scholarly debate, and whether implementing voter ID requirements leads to a decrease in racial minority turnout is still open to dispute. Some scholars have found a decrease (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/716282) in racial minority turnout nationwide (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0731121420966620), but other (https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/136/4/2615/6281042) studies (https://cis.mit.edu/sites/default/files/paper-documents/attnZIPgHeEwYhvId.pdf) have found no effect of voter ID laws on racial minority turnout, and some have even found an increase in youth turnout (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jels.12142).
Beyond minority turnout, the effect of voter ID laws on turnout generally is also unclear. Some studies examined this relationship and found no statistical association between strict ID laws and decreased turnout (Ansolabehere, 2009 (https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096509090313) and Mycoff et al, 2009 (https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096509090301)). However, work by the GAO (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-14-634) has shown a negative correlation between strict photo ID laws and turnout. This finding has been supported by other research (https://bpb-us-w2.wpmucdn.com/web.sas.upenn.edu/dist/7/538/files/2019/07/voter_id_deter.pdf) (Kuk et al, 2020 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21565503.2020.1773280) and Darrah-Okike et al, 2020 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0731121420966620)). Debate continues, since there are methodological challenges to estimating the true causal effects of strict voter identification law, including deficiencies in data quality and sensitivity of results to choices made in statistical estimation (Erikson and Minnite, 2009 (https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/pdf/10.1089/elj.2008.0017?casa_token=_565TxArl2MAAAAA%3A2csuLNY4BFuPkgE1IMoBub4aMfTFUByRrkk6nghb54tcES_5EV4aws65oC-iOe05pF-wBXrqmOA&)and Grimmer et al, 2018 (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/696618?casa_token=ioNmB-0Lh4gAAAAA%3A--esNjcQkkMbN8FvKDyqbQvUhzMB9LcRoxzfJ3jAKe-0BbYZGr8E2sm1TYDhZ_gohsAOTVi4MFzS)).
While it may seem logical that voter ID laws serve to depress turnout (even if descriptively and not causally), some scholars argue (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/pops.12332/full) that the very presence of voter ID laws can have a counter-mobilizing effect that encourages greater turnout among voting populations that are impacted by those laws.
Another important research issue is whether ID laws are implemented consistently as written. Based on studies involving close observation of poll workers, at least two articles (Cobb et al, 2012 (https://www.nowpublishers.com/article/Details/QJPS-10098)and Atkeson et al, 2010 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261379409000912?via%3Dihub)) suggest that inconsistent implementation may be common.
One other aspect of voter ID laws is their effect on the confidence of voters. Research into this question has been partially inspired by the Supreme Court’s argument in Marion County that a rational justification for a state passing a strict ID law is to instill greater confidence in the electoral process. However, the research conducted on this question (Stewart III et al, 2016 (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf)) has not found a consistent correlation between the presence of strict ID laws in a state and an increase in voter confidence (or a decrease in the belief that fraud is rampant).

The presidential election of 2000 and the highly controversial recount in Florida brought the term “voter confidence” into the political lexicon. However, the rhetorical pull of the term “voter confidence” is much stronger than proof of any actual empirical relationship between voter confidence and voter turnout.
This explainer was last updated on May 13, 2026.
Introduction
In the summer of 2001, the National Commission on Federal Election Reform issued its report, To Ensure Pride and Confidence in American Elections (http://web1.millercenter.org/commissions/comm_2001.pdf). Seven years later, when the U.S. Supreme Court (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/07pdf/07-21.pdf)decided in Crawford v. Marion County Board of Elections that strict photo voter ID laws were constitutional, Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that “public confidence in the integrity of the electoral process has independent significance because it encourages citizen participation in the democratic process.” In the aftermath of the 2020 elections, many state legislatures considered a variety of restrictive election laws, including in Georgia. In the remarks he made after signing SB 202, Governor Brian Kemp stated (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1szW8XH2mrw), "There’s no doubt there were many alarming issues with how the election was handled, and those problems understandably led to a crisis of confidence in the ballot box here in Georgia."
Viewing voter confidence as a measure of the quality of American elections and assuming that it is linked to the willingness of Americans to vote are intuitively appealing. However, research finds only a weak causal connection between voter confidence and voter turnout—it has not found clear causal evidence that certain high-profile election administration practices, such as voter ID laws, affect voter confidence.
Surveys have measured public opinion about voter confidence for over two decades. The strongest influence on voter confidence in such surveys, regardless of how the question is asked, is whether the candidate one supports has won or lost an election. This is known as the “winner-loser effect (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1089/elj.2022.0055).”Beyond this phenomenon, voter confidence has been found to be influenced to a lesser degree by other factors, including the intensity of partisan competition and the experience of casting ballots.
Measuring Confidence
When measuring anything, it's important to consider what exact concept is being measured and whether the measurement approach actually captures it. When we try to measure the confidence of voters, we need to ask exactly what they're confident about: that the election was fair? That the votes were counted as they were cast?
When political scientists study voter confidence, they ask voters some variant of the question, “Do you believe that votes in the most recent election were counted as cast?” This question focuses on the mechanics of marking a ballot and having it counted accurately, which is narrower than asking whether the last election was fair—and asking whether the last election was fair is narrower than asking whether “elections in America are usually fair.”
Within this specific academic context, answers about voter confidence are fairly consistent regardless of the precise wording of the question. However, there is one important exception to this pattern of consistency: when survey respondents are asked about their confidence in the parts of the electoral process with which they have direct contact, such as their own vote, they are much more confident than when asked about parts of the electoral process they have indirect contact with, such as the process in the nation as a whole. One consequence of this is that in political debates involving voter confidence, it is possible to cherry-pick survey research in support of arguments that voters either have high levels of confidence in American politics or do not.
Here's an example of how degrees of voter confidence vary with the degree of direct voter contact with the process. In the MIT module of the 2020 Cooperative Election Study (https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/QNZ3F2) (CES), respondents were asked the following question before the election: “How confident are you that your vote in the General Election will be as you intend?” They were also asked, “How confident are you that votes in [your county/your state/nationwide] will be counted as voters intend?” The response categories were very confident, somewhat confident, not too confident, not at all confident, and don’t know.
Looking at the responses to these questions (Figure 1), two patterns immediately jump out. First, regardless of the target of the question (“your vote,” the “local vote,” etc.), confidence was greater after the election than before. For instance, the percentage of voters who said they were very confident their vote would be counted as they intended was 38% before the election, but this jumped to 61% when asked after the election.
Figure 1 shows levels of voter confidence before and after the 2020 general election. These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.

These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.
Second, confidence was greatest—both before and after the election—as the target of the question got closer to the voter. For instance, while 38% of respondents overall were very confident their own vote would be counted as intended in the pre-election survey, 35% were very confident that votes would be counted as intended in their own county or community. These percentages dropped to 29% and 15% when the question asked about the state and the nation, respectively.
Questions about the mechanical aspects of voting tend to elicit more optimistic responses in public-opinion surveys than vague questions about the honesty of elections. For instance, immediately before the 2016 election, the Gallup organization (http://news.gallup.com/poll/196976/update-americans-confidence-voting-election.aspx) asked respondents, “How confident are you that, across the country, the votes will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election?” To this question, 69% responded that they were either very or somewhat confident. However, the poll also asked about how much confidence they had in the “honesty of elections.” Here, only 30% answered that they were confident.
Looking at more recent data, these trends remain. After the 2024 presidential election, the 2024 Survey of the Performance of American Elections (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/projects/survey-performance-american-elections) asked respondents to answer the same voter confidence questions as the 2020 CES MIT module, and the results were unsurprising given the previous years’ data. Nearly 70% of respondents said that they were “very confident” that their own vote was counted as intended in 2024, and this proportion decreased as respondents were asked about their confidence in the vote-counting process in their county/city, state, and nationwide.
Figure 2 shows levels of voter confidence after the 2024 general election. These “levels” are “very confident”, “somewhat confident”, “not too confident”, “not at all confident”, and “don’t know.” The graph displays voter confidence across several stages: confidence that votes were counted accurately in their local area, in their state, and nationwide, as well as confidence that their own vote was counted correctly.

Confidence and outcomes
We've already seen that answers to voter-confidence survey questions vary as the target of the question changes. What else affects voter confidence? The main answer points us in two directions related to political outcomes—who wins, and how close elections are.
The “winner-loser effect” is illustrated by the changing answers to voter confidence questions since they were first asked in 2000. Figure 3 shows the percentage of respondents who reported they were very confident their vote was counted as intended in the Survey of the Performance of American Elections, which was conducted immediately after the 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections. The data for prior elections shows the percentages taken from commercial public opinion polls and reported in research by Michael Sances and Charles Stewart III (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.electstud.2015.08.004).

The overall proportion for these years is shown along with the party breakdown for Democrats and Republicans.

In the first two elections, Republicans were more likely by a margin of 20 percentage points to say they were confident that their vote was counted as intended. The relative opinions of Democrats and Republicans switched in 2008 and became even more entrenched in 2012. Republican confidence rebounded in 2016 while Democratic confidence sagged.
All the major changes in confidence correspond with changes in the parties’ electoral fortunes. This pattern held in 2020, but we observed the largest partisan gap to date at 32 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans. This can likely be attributed to President Trump’s attempts to cast doubt on the results. (Surveyed Republicans cited Trump as their primary source for believing fraud occurred (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/republicans-belief-voter-fraud-opinion-poll/)). In 2024, this partisan gap dramatically shrank as the percentage of very confident Republicans increased by about 20 percentage points and the percentage of very confident Democrats decreased by more than 10 percentage points. This is likely due to Republicans feeling more confident about elections after President Trump won and Democrats experiencing a dip in trust after Harris lost. According to a report by the Yankelovich Center at UCSD (https://yankelovichcenter.ucsd.edu/_files/reports/How-Did-Trust-in-Elections-Change-After-the-2024-Presidential-Contest_.pdf), the narrowing of this partisan gap was mostly driven by higher levels of trust among Republican voters after the 2024 election. Despite increased party polarization, notice that the overall average level of voter confidence has not changed very much across the past six elections.
Voter confidence is also influenced by the sniping that goes on between candidates in the heat of their campaigns. In a close contest, it's common for both sides to accuse the other of dirty tricks. The effects of such attacks are evident when we asked respondents whether votes in their own state were counted as intended. The two lines display the relationship between the points in states that Harris lost (left) and Harris won (right), respectively. Note that regardless of the winner, the closer the elections are (proximity to 50% on the x-axis), the less confident voters are in the result.

Two lines are drawn to show the trend for states that Harris won and states that Harris lost.

Confidence and administration
It's common to justify election reforms by arguing they will increase voter confidence in the electoral system. However, there's little evidence that election administration has a direct effect on voter confidence. The major exception to this statement is that voters who experience problems at polling places tend to be less confident than voters who don’t.
The issue of voter confidence and election reforms has been front and center in justifications for stricter voter ID laws. (If you want to read more about this issue in detail, please see our Voter ID explainer (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification).) As noted above, Justice Stevens’s decision justifying the constitutionality of strict voter ID laws in Crawford v. Marion County Board of Elections credited Indiana’s argument that strict voter ID laws could increase voter confidence. However, subsequent research on this question by Stephen Ansolabehere (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7), Shaun Bowler (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062), Nathaniel Persily (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults), and Charles Stewart III (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals) reveals no correlation between the adoption of strict voter ID laws and increases in voter confidence (Ansolabehere 2009 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/effects-of-identification-requirements-on-votingevidence-from-the-experiences-of-voters-on-electionday/7E19799BF65B5E1AA38BCC3EB9BD83A7); Ansolabehere and Persily 2007 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults); Bowler et al. 2015 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261379415000062); (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?collection=journals&handle=hein.journals/hlr121&id=1760&men_tab=srchresults)Stewart et al. 2016 (https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/stflr68&div=38&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals)). U.S. states increasingly require identification to vote – an ostensive attempt to deter fraud that prompts complaints of selective disenfranchisement. Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation. These results hold through a large number of specifications. Our most demanding specification controls for state, year, and voter fixed effects, along with state and voter time-varying controls. Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95 percent confidence intervals of [-2.3; 2.1pp] and [-3.0; 2.8pp], respectively), and +1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites (with a 95 percent confidence interval of [-0.5; 3.2pp]). The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement. However, the likelihood that non-white voters were contacted by a campaign increases by 4.7 percentage points, suggesting that parties’ mobilization might have offset modest effects of the laws on the participation of ethnic minorities. Finally, strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud – actual or perceived. Overall, our findings suggest that efforts to improve elections may be better directed at other reforms.
